definition: Insidious means gradually harmful while seeming harmless.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word insidious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know insidious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The ivy seemed a charming touch on the brick until its insidious runners worked under the shingles and pried them loose.
Sneaky is small-scale and almost playful—a cookie goes missing; insidious raises the stakes to real harm spreading quietly.
Malignant outranks insidious: insidious harm hides behind a harmless surface, while malignant names something actively destructive and spreading, whether hidden or in plain sight.

Creeping describes any change that advances little by little — creeping costs, creeping doubt — and it stops at the slow pace. Insidious keeps the slowness but adds the menace: the harm builds behind a harmless face, so nothing warns you. A creeping change can be neutral; insidious never is.

A lurking danger is present but hidden and still waiting — the shark beneath the swimmers has not yet done anything. Insidious harm is past waiting: it is already quietly at work, doing damage while everything looks fine. Lurking threatens; insidious harms while it hides.

Insidious means gradually harmful while seeming harmless.
The 'no payments for six months' offer looked like a gift.
It was insidious: interest accrued silently from day one, so by the first bill the debt had already swollen by a fifth, and each minimum payment barely covered the month's new interest.
Nothing about the loan ever felt dangerous—that was the design.
Insidious says more than 'harmful': it means the harm advances gradually behind a harmless face.
A brake that snaps is dangerous; a brake that fades a little each month while feeling fine is insidious.
Insidious is for harm that advances gradually while looking harmless—diseases, debts, habits, rumors.
Devious, its neighbor in this unit, blames a schemer's indirect methods; insidious blames the danger itself, which may have no schemer at all.
If the harm is loud and immediate, insidious is the wrong word no matter how bad the damage.

insidious: Malignant outranks insidious: insidious harm hides behind a harmless surface, while malignant names something actively destructive and spreading, whether hidden or in plain sight.
When water hyacinth first appeared on Lake Naivasha, fishermen picked the lavender flowers for their kitchen tables.
The plant seemed purely ornamental, and that was what made it insidious: nothing about a floating blossom announces a threat.
Each mat of flowers doubled quietly, shading out the algae that fed the fish and pulling oxygen from the water beneath.
For three seasons the catches thinned so gradually that every crew blamed its own luck.
By the time the county sent for help, a third of the bay wore a green lid, and the harm had been done under the prettiest surface imaginable.
